title: Mud crab

identification.basis: The dictionary defines kiju as 'mudcrab', and the Eastern Kuku Yalanji IPA plan uses kiju for the mud crab of the mangroves and mudflats. The giant mud crab, Scylla serrata, is the mud crab of these coasts. Whether kiju also covers any other mud crab species has not been recorded.

summary: **[Kiju](word:kiju)** is the Kuku Yalanji word for the mud crab [ref:hershberger1982], the big, heavy-clawed crab of the mangroves (*Scylla serrata*) [ref:ag2024]. Eastern Kuku Yalanji Traditional Owners name kiju among the important food animals that breed in their [mangrove](entry:mangroves) and mudflat country [ref:jabalbina2016]. Kuku Yalanji families still hunt crabs on the low-tide flats and mangroves of their coast, as at Cooya Beach north of Port Douglas [ref:tpd-walkers]. Crabbing ground is also [crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile), [stingray](entry:stingrays) and stonefish ground, so go at the right tide and watch where you put your feet [ref:crocwise] [ref:healthdirect].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary gives **[kiju](word:kiju)** 'mudcrab' [ref:hershberger1982], and the Eastern Kuku Yalanji sea country plan uses the same word [ref:jabalbina2016]. Other crabs on the same coast have their own names: **[karruku](word:karruku)** 'ghost crab, fiddler crab', **[ngalngal](word:ngalngal)** 'sand crab', **[wuli-wuli](word:wuli-wuli)** 'soldier crab' and **[wurru-bulan](word:wurru-bulan)** 'small crab found on reef' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: The giant mud crab, also called the green mud crab, is an armour-plated crab with **massive, bone-crunching claws**, which it holds out in front of itself like shears [ref:ag2024]. In warm northern waters, where it grows fast and stays active all year, it can weigh nearly 3 kg and measure almost 30 cm across the shell. A young crab only 8 cm across can already bite with a force of up to 40 kg [ref:ag2024]. Mud crabs live 3–4 years. As they grow they moult, swapping the old shell for a soft new one that hardens over a few days [ref:ag2024].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: Giant mud crabs live in [mangroves](entry:mangroves), mudflats and estuaries, coming out of their muddy holes and hides as the tide ebbs and flows to forage for shellfish, other crabs and carrion [ref:ag2024]. In Australia they range from Exmouth Gulf in Western Australia across the north and down the east coast into southern New South Wales [ref:ag2024].

sections.heading: Seasons and tides
sections.body:
In the warm north mud crabs stay active all year [ref:ag2024]. What matters more is the **tide**. Crabbing is done at **[ngajal](word:ngajal)**, low tide, when the flats are exposed [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:tpd-walkers]. Watch for **[balar](word:balar)**, high tide, coming back in [ref:hershberger1982].

Crabs are most vulnerable while their new shell is soft after a moult, and that is also when females are most often mated. Egg-bearing females can carry up to five million eggs, and some travel 100 km or more out to sea to release them [ref:ag2024].

Just north of Kuku Yalanji country, at Cape Bedford, Roth was told that crabs are only good when caught **at the full moon** [ref:roth1901]. He did not record the same belief on the Bloomfield.

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
Kiju is food, and a favourite one.

Roth found that in many North Queensland districts crabs were hunted mainly by **women and young people** [ref:roth1901]. Crabs were also handy as bait: on the Tully River small crabs were sometimes tied on as [fish bait](entry:hooks-and-lines) [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: How kiju are caught and cooked
sections.body:
Neither Roth nor the dictionary describes a Bloomfield crabbing method step by step. The steps below follow how Kuku Yalanji families hunt today at Cooya Beach, plus what the records say about carrying and cooking.

1. **Go at low tide** (*[ngajal](word:ngajal)*), when the flats and [mangrove](entry:mangroves) edges are uncovered [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:tpd-walkers].
2. **Walk the mudflats, tidal lagoons and mangrove edges.** Mud crabs come out of their muddy holes and hides as the tide moves [ref:ag2024].
3. **Take a spear.** At Cooya Beach Kuku Yalanji hunters walk the flats with light bamboo [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) and spear crabs and fish at low tide [ref:tpd-walkers].
4. **Mind the claws.** Even a young crab 8 cm across can bite with a force of up to 40 kg [ref:ag2024].
5. **Check it is legal to keep.** Under Queensland rules only males measuring at least 15 cm across the shell may be kept [ref:qld-limits].
6. **Carry them so they don't fight.** Around Brisbane (far to the south) Roth recorded crabs carried in a [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) with leafy mangrove twigs, which were believed to stop them nipping each other [ref:roth1904].
7. **Cook.** In North Queensland most shellfish were roasted in the ashes, and shrimps and prawns were baked wrapped in wild-ginger leaves or [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark) [ref:roth1901]. The everyday cooking words are *[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals' and *[kurrma](word:kurrma)* '[earth oven](entry:earth-oven)' [ref:hershberger1982]. At Cooya Beach the day's crab is cooked up at home and shared with damper [ref:tpd-walkers].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Crocodiles.** [Mangrove](entry:mangroves) creeks and mudflats are bilngkumu country. Don't wade into creeks or channels, stay back from deep edges, take extra care at dusk, dawn and night, and stay away from crocodile slides and tracks [ref:crocwise].

**Stingrays and stonefish.** Stonefish look like rocks and lie among rocks or in mud or sand, along the coast and in some fresh waters. The spines on their backs carry a dangerous venom [ref:healthdirect]. Stingrays (*[yawu](word:yawu)*) [ref:hershberger1982] carry a barbed spine. To protect yourself [ref:healthdirect]:

1. Enter the water slowly and **shuffle your feet**, which gives [stingrays](entry:stingrays) time to swim away.
2. Don't touch sea creatures.
3. For a stonefish or stinging-fish injury: **call 000** and soak the wound in hot water, no hotter than can easily be tolerated, to ease the pain.

**Mud and tide.** The dictionary has words for a hazard every crabber knows: *[kurndal](word:kurndal)* 'sink in mud or water' and *[yurru-janjil](word:yurru-janjil)* 'suck down, as in quicksand or mud' [ref:hershberger1982]. Know when the tide turns, and don't get cut off on the far side of a channel.

**The crab itself.** The claws can break a finger [ref:ag2024].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Queensland rules.** Mud crabs must measure at least **15 cm**. The limit is **7 per person, or 14 per boat** with two or more people aboard. **No female mud crabs** may be taken, and you cannot keep a crab with its shell missing, or claws without the rest of the crab. Waters closed to crabbing also apply [ref:qld-limits].

**Native title and sea country.** Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders may fish and gather on their country for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993], and the Marine Park's zoning plan recognises this right in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park [ref:gbrmpa-tu]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission.

locations.summary: **There are no mud crabs on the Hann.** Mud crabs live in mangroves, mudflats and estuaries, the Hann is a freshwater river that runs into the North Kennedy [ref:wp-hann], and the Atlas of Living Australia has no mud-crab record in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ag2024] [ref:ala-hann-crab]. The nearest mud-crab country is the mangrove coast of Princess Charlotte Bay, where the Laura Basin's rivers end [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture] [ref:qld-fha-pcb]. The Hann's own crustaceans are the freshwater ones; see [cherabin](entry:cherabin).

sections.heading: The crab country downstream
sections.body: In northern Rinyirru, 'mangrove forest dominates the coastal flats and saltpans in the northern coastal sections' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]. Offshore of it, the Princess Charlotte Bay declared Fish Habitat Area covers 122,530 ha; mud crab is among its fisheries species, and the area has 'commercial, recreational and Indigenous fisheries significance' [ref:qld-fha-pcb]. Rinyirru's Traditional Owners are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. No published record describes how they took mud crabs.

sections.heading: A sign in the trees
sections.body: Kuku Thaypan Elders read the milky pine, **Ku njarl**: 'When the flower blooms crabs are fat' [ref:standley2019]. The record does not say which crab.

sections.heading: The freshwater crustaceans here
sections.body: On the upper Hann the Court recorded a Possum man's evidence that 'he can find Cheribin and freshwater crayfish' [ref:fca-possum]. Around 1900 Roth recorded that 'crayfish are caught with the hands, in nets, or, as on the Musgrave, etc., in logs' [ref:roth1901]. See [cherabin](entry:cherabin).

locations.summary: No mud crabs on the upper Mitchell: they are animals of the tidal mangroves, hundreds of kilometres downstream [ref:ag2024].

sections.heading: Not here
sections.body: Mud crabs are animals of the tidal mangroves [ref:ag2024], so they are not found on the upper Mitchell around Mount Carbine. On the Gulf side you would have to go down to the Mitchell's mangrove estuaries.

locations.summary: This is kiju country: the mangroves and mudflats of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji coast, from the Daintree to the Bloomfield, where families still hunt crabs at low tide [ref:jabalbina2016] [ref:tpd-walkers].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, the mangrove and mudflat areas are 'very important breeding areas' for fish and for kiju, saltwater [mussels](entry:mussels) and a worm that lives in dead mangrove trunks [ref:jabalbina2016]. The flats, mangroves and tidal lagoons at Cooya Beach are traditional Kuku Yalanji fishing grounds [ref:tpd-walkers].

sections.heading: How people use it here
sections.body: The Traditional Owners' plan lists it with the [oysters](entry:oysters), pipis, razor shells and periwinkles of the rocks and beaches as important coastal foods [ref:jabalbina2016]. At Cooya Beach, Kuku Yalanji families still hunt, cook and share crabs together and pass the skills down the generations [ref:tpd-walkers].

sections.heading: Staying safe here
sections.body: Eastern Kuku Yalanji Traditional Owners report that [saltwater crocodiles](entry:saltwater-crocodile) are increasing and becoming more dangerous, especially in the Bloomfield River [ref:jabalbina2016].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Eastern Kuku Yalanji native title was recognised in August 2026 over about 217,884 ha from the Annan River to the Daintree River, including Cow Bay, Thornton Beach and Cape Tribulation [ref:nit2026eky]. One good way to learn crabbing on country is with a Kuku Yalanji–run tour such as the one at Cooya Beach [ref:tpd-walkers].
